repos.title: Agensh: Scaling Organizational Intelligence to 1,024 Agents
repos.paper_summary:
Agensh is a multi-agent harness that coordinates concurrent LLM workers without a central orchestrator. Each worker executes an asynchronous loop: gathering context, claiming sub-tasks, taking action, verifying results, and merging progress into a shared workspace. Coordination relies on three infrastructure components: a Git-based shared workspace for code integration, a message interface for peer communication, and a shared context board for reusable findings.

The paper evaluates Agensh on the five hardest ProgramBench tasks using GPT-5.6-sol (high) with a 6-hour budget. Scaling from 1 to 128 agents increases the mean final test-pass rate from 19.31% to 28.78%, a 49% relative improvement. On the pandoc task, scaling to 1,024 agents raises the final test-pass rate from 33.89% to 55.06%. Larger organizations also reach comparable performance levels earlier; for instance, 128 agents exceed a 30% pass rate at 30 minutes, while single agents remain below this threshold for two hours. Limitations include reliance on specific underlying models and harnesses, and the need for staggered agent activation to manage scope contention in large-scale deployments.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Agensh replaces a central orchestrator with self-organized workers, and scaling 1 to 128 agents raises mean test-pass rate from 19.31% to 28.78%.

digest_headlines.heading: Multi-Agent Organization Harness
digest_headlines.headline: Each worker repeats a five-step loop over a shared workspace, message interface and shared context, with no central orchestrator.

digest_headlines.heading: Scaling Multi-Agent Organization to 1,024 Agents
digest_headlines.headline: Mean test-pass rate rises with 8, 32 and 128 agents, and pandoc reaches 55.06% with 1,024 agents.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior harnesses keep task assignment under a fixed lead or trained orchestrator, while some tools coordinate workers through shared state.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Agent count is proposed as a new scaling dimension, though every reported run uses one agent model.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix gives the worker prompt, the event-driven runtime, the experiment configuration and the staggered agent launch schedule.

repos.title: LEANN: A Low-Storage Vector Index
repos.paper_summary:
LEANN is a storage-efficient vector index that recomputes embeddings at query time instead of storing them, and prunes the proximity graph while keeping high-degree hub nodes. It builds on HNSW and FAISS. A two-level search uses approximate product-quantization (PQ) distances to select candidates for exact recomputation, and dynamic batching groups recomputations across exploration steps (target batch of 64) to improve GPU use. High-degree preserving pruning keeps the top 2% of nodes by degree at maximum degree M and caps other nodes at M/5.

On a 76 GB text corpus (RPJ-Wiki) with Qwen3-4B on an RTX 4090, LEANN uses 4 GB of storage versus 188 GB for HNSW and 20 GB for PQ. End-to-end RAG latency is 23.3 s for LEANN and 21.0 s for HNSW, with 25.5% downstream accuracy for both. Table 2 reports retrieval latency at 90% recall across NQ, GPQA, TriviaQA, and HotpotQA.

Limitations: search latency rises from milliseconds to seconds, which the paper accepts because generation dominates RAG latency. Some baselines (HNSW, IVF) ran on a larger-memory server.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Graph indices for a 76 GB corpus need 188 GB, too large for personal devices, so a smaller index is needed.

digest_headlines.heading: Background
digest_headlines.headline: Proximity graph indices need few distance computations, but storage has two parts: vectors and index metadata.

digest_headlines.heading: LEANN Overview
digest_headlines.headline: LEANN keeps a pruned graph and product-quantized codes, recomputing exact embeddings during queries.

digest_headlines.heading: Graph-based Recomputation
digest_headlines.headline: Two-level search and dynamic batching cut recomputation while keeping exact distances for selected candidates.

digest_headlines.heading: Compact Graph Structure
digest_headlines.headline: Preserving edges of the top 2% high-degree nodes shrinks graph metadata while maintaining high retrieval accuracy.

digest_headlines.heading: Index Building and Update
digest_headlines.headline: Sharded construction and buffered updates limit peak storage during index building and modification.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: LEANN matches the accuracy of the standard graph index at 90% recall while storing about 5% of raw data size.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Earlier systems reduce memory via disk layouts, quantization or online embedding but still store embeddings.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusions
digest_headlines.headline: LEANN keeps the index under 5% of raw data size, up to 50 times smaller than existing methods, with high recall.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers relative neighborhood graph pruning, update algorithms, Mac latency, and ablations on construction, embedding model, caching, and latency breakdown.

repos.title: LMCache: An Efficient KV Cache Layer for Enterprise-Scale LLM Inference
repos.paper_summary: LMCache is an open-source library that extracts, stores, and transfers KV caches for LLM inference engines like vLLM and SGLang. It supports cross-query prefix caching and prefill-decode disaggregation by moving data between GPU memory, CPU DRAM, local disks, and remote storage. The system optimizes data movement using batched operations with configurable chunk sizes, layer-wise pipelining to overlap compute and I/O, and zero-copy mechanisms to minimize data duplication. A modular connector interface decouples LMCache from the evolving APIs of inference engines. In evaluations on H100 GPUs across six models, LMCache achieves up to 15× higher throughput and 2× lower latency compared to basic vLLM and commercial baselines. For prefill-decode disaggregation, it reduces mean time-to-first-token by 1.53–1.84× relative to native vLLM implementation. Limitations include reduced effectiveness at low network bandwidths; loading from remote storage only outperforms full prefill when input contexts exceed 256K tokens at 32 Gbps bandwidth. Additionally, context truncation in production environments can reduce prefix cache hit rates by half.

repos.title: Reinforcement Learning for Versatile, Dynamic, and Robust Bipedal Locomotion Control
repos.paper_summary: This paper presents a dual-history reinforcement learning controller for bipedal robots, enabling diverse locomotion skills including walking, running, and jumping on the Cassie robot. The method uses a long-term input/output history encoder to adapt to dynamics changes and contact events, combined with a short-term history fed directly to the policy network to handle high-frequency control needs. Training follows a three-stage curriculum: single-task learning, task randomization, and dynamics randomization. In simulation ablations, the dual-history architecture outperforms baselines like RMA and state-feedback-only policies under randomized dynamics parameters. Real-world experiments demonstrate zero-shot sim-to-real transfer, with the robot maintaining stable standing for 459 days, completing a 400-meter dash, and executing jumps up to 1.4 meters forward and 0.44 meters high. The authors identify task randomization as a key source of robustness distinct from dynamics randomization, promoting compliant recovery behaviors. Limitations include difficulty achieving precise velocity tracking during fast running and the requirement for specific reference motions; for instance, backward jumps could not be learned from a forward-jumping reference alone.

repos.title: VisSearch-Bench: Evaluating Long Horizon Visual Search in Multimodal Agents
repos.paper_summary: VisSearch-Bench is a benchmark of 204 human-written tasks for evaluating visual context management in long-horizon open-web search by multimodal agents. The tasks span five categories: Set-wise Visual Search, Sequential Visual Search, Hybrid Wide–Deep Search, Competitive Visual Disambiguation, and Visual-Structure-Guided Search, across 7 primary and 25 secondary domains. Annotators build each task from public sources with a reference answer and traceable evidence, and automated checks plus human review remove tasks that can be solved without the visual evidence. Accuracy requires the predicted answer to contain all and only the required content. Process Score is the fraction of labeled critical states recovered, averaged over tasks. Across 16 models and agent setups, the best system reaches 26.47% accuracy, a ReAct agent with Kimi-K3. Direct answering by GPT-5.5 scores 6.37%, and ReAct with GPT-5.5 reaches 25.49%. Several open-source models score 0.00% accuracy on the direct setting. The paper states that the benchmark's 204 tasks are a limited sample and that the construction relies on human annotation.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Some search tasks use images only to identify an entity, so the paper tests how agents link visual evidence across steps.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: VisSearch-Bench is the only listed benchmark that covers set answers, evidence links, and partial credit together.

digest_headlines.heading: VisSearch-Bench
digest_headlines.headline: Each of 204 tasks is built from public sources with traceable evidence, a locked answer, and human review.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Search lifts accuracy well above direct answering, but the best system still fully solves only 26.47% of tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Verifying multiple objects and combining findings into consistent answers remain open challenges for multimodal search agents.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists related benchmark details, prompts, hyperparameters, release fields, and seventeen case-study trajectories.

repos.title: Monocular Identity-Conditioned Facial Reflectance Reconstruction
repos.paper_summary: ID2Reflectance is a framework for monocular facial reflectance reconstruction that estimates diffuse albedo, specular albedo, roughness, and surface normal maps from a single in-the-wild image. The method learns a facial prior in image space rather than UV space to reduce dependency on limited light-stage data. It trains a VQGAN with multi-domain codebooks, aligning RGB and reflectance domains by jointly training on FFHQ and 135 captured subjects. An identity-conditioned swapper module, trained on VGGFace2HQ using AdaIN, injects identity features from the target image into the pre-trained decoder. At inference, the system synthesizes three-view reflectance images and stitches them into UV-space maps. On a test set of 20 subjects, ID2Reflectance achieves a PSNR of 28.47 dB for diffuse albedo, outperforming TRUST (21.63 dB) and ID2Albedo (23.72 dB). Identity similarity reaches 0.735 compared to 0.532 for ID2Albedo. The total inference time is 3.8 seconds per face on an A6000 GPU. The paper notes that reconstructed PBR maps may not be physically plausible due to the lack of ground-truth supervision.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Reflectance models trained on few light-stage captures generalize poorly, so the method learns the reflectance prior in image space from abundant RGB faces.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior facial reflectance methods depend on light-stage data and their data is unreleased, while face swapping methods target only the RGB domain.

digest_headlines.heading: Methodology
digest_headlines.headline: Two-stage codebook training aligns reflectance with RGB, so identity swapping learned on RGB transfers to reflectance maps.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Trained on 115 captured subjects, the method gives identity-preserved reflectance on Digital Emily and in-the-wild faces in 3.8 seconds/face.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusions and Discussions
digest_headlines.headline: The paper concludes that limited captured data yields a reliable reflectance prior and notes the method could be misused.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers the light stage rig, public datasets, codebook and swapper details, UV stitching, a fairness benchmark, and further qualitative results.

repos.title: REMORY: Learning Residual Memory for Context Compaction
repos.paper_summary: Remory is a learned memory network that adds a bounded set of continuous soft tokens after a textual compaction summary, so a frozen LLM can approximate its continuation with the full history. The network is conditioned on the summary and emits 64 tokens per block of up to 1,024 source positions, capped at 4,096 slots. Training has two stages: reconstruction of source passages, then summary-conditioned continuation, using reverse KL against a teacher that sees the full history. On SummHay (92 queries, Qwen3.8-27B), summary plus memory raises citation F1 from 56.98 to 61.03 and joint score from 39.84 to 43.39, with coverage nearly unchanged (67.55 to 67.95), using 5.2% of raw-context positions. Within-actor agent runs improve: Qwen AutomationBench rises from 35.5 to 45.3, Terminal-Bench 2.1 from 71.9 to 76.4, and BrowseComp from 74.0 to 77.0. Limitations: the 95% bootstrap interval for the SummHay joint-score gain is [+0.74, +6.21]; Terminal-Bench and BrowseComp use one run per configuration; cost estimates exclude memory-network execution; and the first-action preference judgments do not measure outcomes.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Summaries alone may miss context needed later, so Remory adds learned memory tokens after a summary.

digest_headlines.heading: Residual Memory
digest_headlines.headline: A memory network trains soft tokens so a frozen actor matches its full-history continuation.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Residual memory raises SummHay joint score and agent scores while reducing repeated tool outputs and errors.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Remory extends summary-plus-retrieval memory with a continuous representation learned from the checkpoint.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Attribution, agent scores, and preferred next actions support the residual formulation as a bounded supplement.

repos.title: Gradio: Hassle-Free Sharing and Testing of ML Models in the Wild
repos.paper_summary:
Gradio is an open-source Python package that generates a web-based interface for machine learning models, allowing non-technical users to test them via a shared URL. The system supports inputs and outputs for images, text, and audio, and is compatible with Scikit-Learn, TensorFlow, PyTorch, or arbitrary Python functions. When a researcher launches the interface, Gradio creates an SSH tunnel to host the model on the original machine, enabling remote collaborators to access it through a browser without installing software. Users can manipulate inputs, such as cropping or occluding image regions, and flag incorrect predictions to send feedback directly to the developer.

The authors validated the tool in a pilot study involving an ML researcher and a cardiologist classifying echocardiograms for pacemaker presence. The underlying model achieved an AUC of 0.93. Setup took approximately 10 minutes. During testing, the cardiologist successfully identified model failures by flipping images vertically and used the built-in tools to verify predictions by occluding the pacemaker. Limitations include the study's small scope of one user pair over a short period, and the absence of quantitative measures for trust or satisfaction.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Domain experts usually cannot try ML models during development, so the authors built Gradio, a Python package that generates web interfaces.

digest_headlines.heading: Motivation
digest_headlines.headline: Interviews with 12 ML researchers yielded four design requirements for interfaces, sharing, input manipulation, and notebook embedding.

digest_headlines.heading: Implementation
digest_headlines.headline: Gradio wraps a trained model in an Interface object with four required parameters and shares it through a secure tunnel.

digest_headlines.heading: Pilot Study: Echocardiogram Classification
digest_headlines.headline: A single pilot pair found the shared link let a cardiologist probe a pacemaker classifier and flag failures.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion & Next Steps
digest_headlines.headline: The authors expect the package to widen domain expert access, but a single short pair study cannot establish usefulness.

repos.title: L3G-World: Real-Time Infinite World Generation with Latent 3D Gaussian Memory
repos.paper_summary: L3G-World is a real-time world-generation framework built on a Latent 3D Gaussian Memory (L3G): 3D Gaussians that each store a VAE latent feature and are updated as video is generated. The memory updater, L3G-Mem, spawns Gaussians only where the rendered memory has low opacity or high RGB error, and refines visible Gaussians with residual updates. The video diffusion transformer, L3G-Gen, conditions on the memory rendered in VAE latent space, avoiding decode-and-re-encode. L3G-Gen is trained with rectified flow and distilled to a few-step student with AnyFlow, reaching 9.02 FPS on one H100. Against the most efficient prior explicit 3D-memory baseline per metric, the paper reports 26.7–38.9× fewer 3D primitives, 3.0–3.2× faster memory reconstruction, and 349–359× higher VAE-space rendering throughput. Baselines include GEN3C, Lyra 2.0, Spatia, NeoVerse, Yume 1.5 and Matrix-Game 3.0; training uses DL3DV and RealEstate10K. The provided text ends before the quality tables, so the generation-quality claims are unverified here. Limitations: memory depends on Depth Anything 3 for metric depth, and speed gains are measured against one baseline per metric.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Interactive world models face a cost-consistency trade-off, and a compact latent Gaussian memory is proposed to address it.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Works
digest_headlines.headline: Prior explicit 3D memories either accumulate dense per-frame primitives or optimize too slowly for real-time generation.

digest_headlines.heading: Methodology
digest_headlines.headline: A memory updater spawns Gaussians in uncovered regions, refines existing ones, and renders VAE latent features directly into the generator.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: On the first of two datasets, L3G-World reaches the highest loop-closure PSNR, 16.00, among the compared methods.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The conclusion presents compact latent 3D memory as a practical foundation for scalable interactive world models.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix gives flow-map and Gaussian preliminaries, training and retrieval details, online reconstruction results, and limitations.
